tailor.intro: Learn tailoring from measurement to finished garment. Master the machine, cut clean patterns, and build a client base that returns.

skillDomains.name: Measurement
skillDomains.description: Every garment is only as good as its measurements.

skills.name: Body Measurement
skills.description: Take accurate measurements that produce garments that fit.

modules.title: The essential measurements
modules.content:
For a basic garment you need:

Upper body

  • Neck
  • Chest/bust
  • Shoulder width
  • Sleeve length
  • Back length

Lower body

  • Waist
  • Hip
  • Inseam
  • Outseam

Take measurements over light clothing. Note posture — it affects fit more than numbers.

modules.title: How to measure correctly
modules.content:
Never guess

Write every number down immediately.

Keep the tape level

Chest, waist, and hip measurements must be horizontal.

Snug, not tight

The tape should sit against the body but not compress it.

Record in inches AND centimetres

Some clients use inches, some cm.

The client's posture

Note asymmetry. Fitting adjustments depend on this.

steps.q: A client's chest measures 40 inches. Should the finished garment chest measure 40?
steps.f: Garments need ease — usually 2-4 inches on chest for a shirt.

steps.q: You've taken measurements and are about to start cutting. What do you check?
o: That you've recorded every number and noted posture
steps.f: Missing measurements mean a wasted cut.

steps.q: A client has one shoulder lower than the other. What do you do?
o: Note it and adjust the pattern accordingly
steps.f: Asymmetric posture requires asymmetric pattern adjustments.

modules.title: Create a measurement chart
modules.prompt: Design a client measurement chart you can reuse for every order.
steps: Include every essential measurement with labels
Add columns for inches and centimetres
Test it by measuring a friend

skillDomains.name: Pattern Cutting
skillDomains.description: Turn measurements into a pattern that becomes a garment.

modules.title: What a pattern is
modules.content:
A pattern is a flat template of the garment pieces, cut to the client's measurements.

Types

  • Block pattern — the base shape with no style
  • Adapted pattern — block pattern modified for a specific style
  • Commercial pattern — pre-made, sold in standard sizes

Professionals keep block patterns for the client's body. Every new style is adapted from the block.

modules.title: Drafting a basic block
modules.content:
To draft a block you need:

  • Pattern paper
  • Ruler and curved ruler
  • Pencil
  • Pins

Steps for a bodice block

  1. Draw a rectangle: chest width × back length
  2. Mark chest line, waist line, hip line
  3. Mark shoulder, neck, and armhole points
  4. Draw curves for armhole and neck
  5. Add darts for bust or waist shaping
  6. Label every piece and add a 1.5cm seam allowance

steps.q: You're adapting a bodice block into a loose-fitting blouse. What changes?
o: Add ease to the pattern width
steps.f: Loose fit needs added ease AND dart removal.

steps.q: How much seam allowance do you add around a pattern piece?
You cut your fabric and notice the grain line is diagonal to the pattern's grain. What's the problem?
o: The garment will hang wrong and twist
steps.f: Grain line matters. Cutting off-grain produces garments that twist.

skillDomains.name: Sewing
skillDomains.description: The machine work that turns fabric into garment.

skills.name: Machine Work
skills.description: Control the machine — don't let it control you.

modules.title: Know your machine
modules.content:
The parts

  • Needle
  • Presser foot
  • Feed dogs
  • Bobbin
  • Tension dial

The basic stitch

The needle carries upper thread through the fabric, a hook catches it, and it locks with the bobbin thread underneath.

Common settings

  • Straight stitch — length 2.5mm, tension 4
  • Zigzag — for knits and finishing edges

modules.title: Tension adjustment
modules.content:
Symptoms of bad tension

  • Loops on top — upper tension too loose
  • Loops underneath — upper tension too tight
  • Thread breaks constantly — tension too tight
  • Puckered fabric — tension too tight or needle too large

How to fix

Adjust the upper tension dial one number at a time and test on scrap fabric.

steps.q: Thread keeps breaking while sewing. Likely cause?
o: Tension too tight, needle too small, or thread caught
steps.f: Breaking thread usually means tension too tight or wrong needle size.

steps.q: The stitch looks fine on top but loopy underneath. What do you adjust?
steps.f: Loops underneath mean upper tension is too tight.

steps.q: Fabric puckers around the stitch. Most likely fix?
o: Loosen tension, reduce stitch length, or change needle
steps.f: Puckering comes from too-tight tension, too-long stitches, or wrong needle.

modules.title: Build a stitch sampler
modules.prompt: Sew a sampler showing at least 8 different seam and finishing techniques.
steps: Cut labelled squares of scrap fabric
Practice each technique on one square
Write one line explaining when to use each
Keep the sampler as a reference

skillDomains.name: Fitting & Finishing
skillDomains.description: The difference between a sewn garment and a wearable one.

skills.name: Fitting
skills.description: Adjust the garment on the client before finishing.

modules.title: Why fitting matters
modules.content:
No pattern is perfect. Every garment needs adjustment after it's basted so it can be fitted on the actual body before final stitching.

The fitting process

  1. Sew the garment together with long basting stitches
  2. Have the client put it on
  3. Pin out excess fabric or adjust seam lines
  4. Mark adjustments with chalk or pins
  5. Take the garment off and re-sew with adjustments
  6. Fit again if needed

steps.q: The garment pulls across the chest when the client crosses their arms. What's the fix?
steps.f: Pulling during movement means not enough ease.

steps.q: The shoulders droop and the sleeve hangs past the shoulder point. What's the fix?
steps.f: Droopy shoulders mean the shoulder width is too wide.

steps.q: The waist is too tight but the hips fit. What do you do?
steps.f: Let out only what needs adjustment.

skills.name: Finishing
skills.description: The final touches that make a garment professional.

modules.title: Finishing is what shows
modules.content:
Two garments can be identical in construction, but one looks cheap and one looks expensive — based entirely on finishing.

What finishing includes

  • Trimming loose threads
  • Pressing every seam as you go
  • Clean inside seams
  • Even hems
  • Secure buttons
  • Neat buttonholes
  • Final press

modules.title: Pressing — the invisible skill
modules.content:
"Sewing is 50% ironing." This is not a joke.

Rules

  • Press every seam after sewing it
  • Use the right temperature for the fabric
  • Press, don't drag
  • Use a pressing cloth on delicate fabrics
  • Use a tailor's ham for curved areas

A well-pressed simple garment looks better than a poorly-pressed complex one.

skillDomains.name: Client Work
skillDomains.description: Consultation, pricing, and building a business.

skills.name: Consultation
skills.description: Understand what the client actually wants.

modules.title: Ask before you cut
modules.content:
A client says "make me a dress". That's not enough information. Ask:

  • What's the occasion?
  • What style do you like? (Ask for photos)
  • What fabric?
  • When do you need it?
  • What's your budget?

Then confirm in writing before you cut anything.

modules.title: Consult a wedding client
modules.prompt: A bride wants a dress for her traditional wedding. She shows you a photo of a style she likes. Describe how you would run the consultation.
modules.context: Weddings are the highest-stakes orders for a tailor.

skills.name: Pricing
skills.description: Price for the work, not for what clients hope to pay.

modules.title: Price the four parts
modules.content:
Every price must cover:

  1. Materials — fabric, thread, buttons, lining
  2. Labour — hours × real hourly rate
  3. Overhead — rent, electricity, machine wear
  4. Margin — 30-50% for tailoring work

Under-pricing is the #1 cause of tailor burnout.

modules.prompt: A client commissions a full traditional outfit (top and trousers). Materials: 25,000 Le fabric, 3,000 Le thread and trims. You estimate 12 hours at 3,000 Le/hour. Overhead: 2,000 Le. You want a 40% margin.
modules.context: Complete outfits are your most profitable orders.
